name: Cyclothymic disorder
dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Bipolar and Related Disorders — Cyclothymic Disorder
summary: A long-running pattern of mood instability: for years, the client moves between milder highs (more energy, confidence or irritability) and milder lows, with few settled stretches, but the swings never reach a full manic or depressive episode. Others may see the client as moody or unpredictable, and relationships, work and finances can suffer from the unevenness. Some people later develop bipolar I or II, so track mood over time. A steady routine, sleep regularity and psychoeducation help; refer for a medication evaluation when swings are disabling. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Ask how many years the ups and downs have gone on and how long the client has felt settled at a stretch. Check the duration thresholds in DSM-5-TR.

ruleOuts.label: Stimulants, steroids and other substances or medicines
ruleOuts.note: Cocaine, amphetamines, high-dose corticosteroids and some antidepressant starts can bring on manic-like states. Review the medication list with the prescriber. This app does not store substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Thyroid, neurological and other medical causes
ruleOuts.note: Hyperthyroidism, brain injury, seizures, multiple sclerosis, dementia and some infections can cause elation, irritability or disinhibition, especially with a first episode after age 40. Arrange a medical work-up.

ruleOuts.label: Primary psychotic disorder
ruleOuts.note: Hallucinations or delusions that persist when mood is level point toward a schizophrenia-spectrum or schizoaffective picture.

ruleOuts.label: Unipolar depression without a history of highs
ruleOuts.note: Ask the client and, with consent, someone who knows them well about past periods of unusual energy, little sleep or risky spending; highs are often missed or remembered as good spells.

specifiers.label: With anxious distress (descriptive)
specifiers.note: Anxiety alongside the swings changes the plan; screen with the GAD-7. See DSM-5-TR for specifiers.

differentials.label: Bipolar II disorder
differentials.distinguishing: At least one full depressive episode and a clear high.

differentials.label: Borderline personality pattern
differentials.distinguishing: Shifts are rapid, tied to relationships, and come with fear of abandonment and identity disturbance.

differentials.label: Persistent depressive disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Years of low mood without the milder highs.

differentials.label: Substance-related mood changes
differentials.distinguishing: Swings follow stimulant, alcohol or cannabis use and withdrawal.

comorbidities.label: Bipolar II disorder
comorbidities.note: Some clients with this pattern later have a full depressive episode; track over time.

comorbidities.label: Alcohol use disorder
comorbidities.note: Alcohol is often used to manage the swings; screen for it.

comorbidities.label: Adult ADHD
comorbidities.note: Restlessness and impulsivity overlap; ADHD is steady rather than cycling.

interventions.name: Psychoeducation and mood tracking
interventions.evidence: Recommended as part of care for bipolar-spectrum conditions in NICE CG185.
interventions.note: Daily mood and sleep tracking makes the pattern visible to client and clinician.

interventions.name: Interpersonal and social rhythm therapy (adjunct)
interventions.evidence: Social rhythm regularity is a core target in IPSRT (Frank et al., 2005); evidence comes mainly from bipolar I.
interventions.note: Stable wake time, meals and activity.

interventions.name: CBT skills for mood swings
interventions.evidence: Adapted from CBT for bipolar disorder; trial evidence in cyclothymia is limited.
interventions.note: Notice early shifts and plan steadying actions.

interventions.name: Referral for medication evaluation
interventions.evidence: Medication decisions rest with a prescriber.
interventions.note: Refer when swings are disabling or move toward full episodes.

culturalNotes: Expressions of energy, religiosity and confidence differ across cultures. Judge a change against the client's own usual self and community norms, not the clinician's.
Black and Latino clients with mood symptoms are more often misdiagnosed with psychotic disorders in US studies. Take a careful mood history before concluding that psychosis is primary.
Shame about psychiatric illness and medication can delay care. Explain that mood episodes are common, treatable and not a character flaw, and ask what the family believes about the cause.
Night shifts, travel across time zones, fasting periods and late-night celebrations can disrupt sleep and routine. Plan around them with the client rather than asking them to give them up.
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, and check that key terms translate with the meaning you intend.

redFlagRules.message: Suicidal thoughts or self-harm are documented in this input. Ask directly about intent, plan and access to means, follow your crisis protocol and build a safety plan with the client; this app never rates risk.
Psychotic symptoms are documented alongside the mood picture. Psychosis during a high or low is a medical priority: arrange an urgent psychiatric evaluation and check safety at home.
